assets.visual_frame_description: A bright community center in Austin, Texas, at 8 a.m. on a Saturday. Maya, the volunteer coordinator, stands at a folding table covered in pledge cards while neighbors file past on their way to the grocery store. To her right hangs a banner reading 'Food Bank Weekend Drive' and a small poster showing a suburban home with a three-inch 'Drive Carefully' sign in its window. As neighbors hesitate, Maya smiles and hands them a pen, pointing at the single small card before gesturing to the much larger volunteer sign-up sheet.
assets.player_mission: You are coaching Maya's campaign to turn reluctant neighbors into full-shift food bank volunteers without coercion. First, study how she uses a tiny first request to open the door to a large one, and identify the evidence that supports this strategy. Then, when participation stalls, select the intervention that chains all three documented influence tactics into a slow ascent into goodness.
key_concepts: The reverse-Milgram experiment is a thought experiment that replaces Milgram's escalating demands to harm with escalating demands to do good, producing a slow ascent into goodness instead of a slow descent into evil.
The foot-in-the-door tactic starts with a small request most people readily perform, then asks for a related but much bigger request that was the actual goal all along.

Freedman and Fraser found that fewer than twenty percent of suburban homeowners agreed to put a big, ugly 'Drive Carefully' sign in their yards, but three-fourths agreed when they had first posted a small three-inch sign in their windows two weeks earlier.
Chaining a series of increasingly larger requests enhances the foot-in-the-door effect, putting two feet in the door rather than just one.

Social models of altruism increase helping: role models have been shown to boost Salvation Army donations, promote helping a stranger with a flat tire, lower aggression, reduce littering, and increase donations to poor children.
Models persuade far more effectively than words: children exposed to an adult who preached charity but practiced greed did what the model did, not what the model said.
Self-labeling of helpfulness works because people adopt behaviors consistent with an assigned identity, just as SPE prisoners and guards took on the manners of their randomly assigned roles.

Researchers found that telling someone he or she is 'a generous person' increases compliance with a request to contribute to multiple-sclerosis prevention, and labeling people 'blood donors' makes them more likely to keep donating.

The Goodness Generator's first button is ten minutes writing a thank-you note or get-well card, then twenty minutes advising a troubled child, then reading to an illiterate housekeeper, then tutoring, babysitting, soup-kitchen work, and helping veterans and orphans.
According to dissonance theory, beliefs follow behavior: get people to perform good actions and they will generate the underlying principles to justify them.
The reverse-Milgram experiment has never actually been done; Zimbardo proposes it as a design for using the power of authority and situation to produce virtue.
The three tactics combined in the reverse-Milgram design are the foot-in-the-door tactic, social modeling, and self-labeling of helpfulness.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the foot-in-the-door compliance tactic: a small initial commitment alters self-perception and paves the way for much larger requests, as demonstrated by Freedman and Fraser's sign study. Combined with social modeling and self-labeling, the same situational machinery that produces evil can be reversed to produce altruism.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The reverse-Milgram experiment converts Milgram's escalating-authority paradigm into a slow ascent into goodness: participants face intensifying demands to help rather than to harm, driven by three documented influence tactics — foot-in-the-door, social modeling, and self-labeling of helpfulness.
assets.stage_1_observation: You watch Maya pitch the food-bank drive. She first asks each neighbor only to sign a pledge card — a tiny request everyone performs — and two weeks later returns to ask for four volunteer hours. On screen, the neighbors who signed cards nod more readily at the big request, while a banner recalls the Freedman and Fraser 'Drive Carefully' yard-sign study and its ratio of small-sign compliance to big-sign compliance.
assets.stage_1_question: Which finding from the chapter justifies Maya's strategy of leading with a small request before the big one?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Freedman and Fraser found that fewer than twenty percent of homeowners agreed to put a big, ugly 'Drive Carefully' sign in their yards, but three-fourths agreed if they had two weeks earlier posted an unobtrusive three-inch sign in their window — small commitments open the door to much larger ones.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The drive stalls at the pledge stage: neighbors signed cards but few signed up for shifts. Maya must escalate commitment without pressure. She can put experienced volunteers visibly sorting cans in the lobby, have the center director greet each pledger by name as a 'generous, altruistic person,' and send a follow-up ask ladder from one hour to a full shift. Choose the intervention that best combines the three reverse-Milgram tactics.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Chain all three tactics: pair pledgers with visible volunteers already working the food bank (social modeling, because models persuade more effectively than words), greet each volunteer by name and label them as generous and altruistic (self-labeling, which makes people act on the identity label), and keep the ask ladder climbing from pledge card to one hour to a full shift as each step is completed (foot-in-the-door chaining, enhanced by successive larger requests).

assets.topic: Frame Vigilance Against the Death Tax Slogan
assets.visual_frame_description: A packed town-hall meeting in a midwestern county building, ceiling fans turning slowly. On the dais, Lena, a young city-council aide, sits beside a stack of policy briefs while a polished lobbyist in a navy suit works the microphone, repeating the phrase 'bureaucratic death tax.' Above the crowd, a ticker caption flashes the chapter's line: 'Who makes the frame becomes the artist, or the con artist.' Residents nod at the slogan while the identical estate-tax policy sits unread in their agendas.
assets.player_mission: You are helping Lena keep the debate honest. First, observe how the lobbyist's framing moves the crowd and identify why a mere name change is so powerful. Then, when Lena takes the microphone, choose the response grounded in the chapter's advice for fighting frame power.
key_concepts: The way issues are framed is often more influential than the persuasive arguments within their boundaries.
Effective frames can seem not to be frames at all — just sound bites, visual images, slogans, and logos — and they influence us without our being conscious of them.
Voters who favored reducing estate-tax benefits for the rich were urged to vote against a 'death tax'; the tax was exactly the same, but its defining term was different.
We desire things that are framed as 'scarce' even when they are plentiful.
We are averse to things framed as potential losses and prefer what is presented as a gain, even when the ratio of positive to negative prognoses is identical.
People reject a 40 percent chance of losing X over Y but accept the 60 percent chance of gaining Y over X, though the underlying ratio is the same.
The linguist George Lakoff shows that it is crucial to be aware of frame power and to be vigilant to offset its insidious influence on emotions, thoughts, and votes.
Frame vigilance is one of the ten steps for resisting unwanted influences, and it requires critical thinking: asking for evidence and separating rhetoric from substance.
The three Ss — self-awareness, situational sensitivity, and street smarts — are the key to resistance, and frame vigilance exercises situational sensitivity.
Critical thinking means rejecting simple solutions as quick fixes for complex personal or social problems and imagining end-game consequences of current practices.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests frame vigilance: the way an issue is framed often outweighs the arguments inside the frame, so relabeling an estate tax as a 'death tax' moves voters without their awareness. The chapter urges active vigilance and reframing in gain terms, drawing on Lakoff's analysis of frame power.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Frame vigilance: whoever makes the frame becomes the artist or the con artist. Frames work below awareness through slogans and labels, so resistance means naming the frame, demanding substance, and recasting the identical policy in gain terms rather than loss terms.
assets.stage_1_observation: The lobbyist tells the crowd that a 'bureaucratic death tax' will confiscate family farms. The policy under discussion is a routine estate-tax adjustment — the exact same tax under a different name. On screen, residents frown at the phrase while Lena's notes remind you that the crowd rejected the identical policy earlier when it was called an 'estate tax.'
assets.stage_1_question: Why is the phrase 'death tax' so potent even though it names the same tax as 'estate tax'?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The frame is often more influential than the persuasive arguments within its boundaries: effective frames seem not to be frames at all, so the defining term shapes orientation without conscious awareness — exactly as when voters who favored reducing estate-tax benefits were urged to oppose a 'death tax.'
assets.stage_2_intervention: Lena takes the microphone as the crowd begins to chant the lobbyist's slogan. She can (a) recite the budget numbers debunking the phrase, (b) name the frame, substitute 'estate tax,' and present the identical ratio as a gain rather than a loss, or (c) ridicule the lobbyist personally. Select the move the chapter's advice supports.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Lena names the frame openly and reframes: she points out that the crowd already supported the identical policy when called an estate tax, and that the slogan exploits the fact that we avoid a 40 percent chance of losing X but accept a 60 percent chance of gaining Y even when the ratio is the same — then restates the policy as a gain. Naming the frame and demanding substance defuses it, since frames influence us only while we are unaware of them.

assets.topic: Just Authority Versus Unjust Authority in a Hospital
assets.visual_frame_description: A dimly lit hospital med room at 11 p.m. Priya, a newly hired nurse in her late twenties, stands between two men: Dr. Feld, the gray-haired attending who has quietly earned thirty years of clinical reputation, and 'Coach Rex,' a polished consultant in a silk tie hired by the administrator to 'optimize throughput.' Rex's flowchart of skipped checklists is taped to the supply cabinet; Dr. Feld's verification binder sits unopened beside it.
assets.player_mission: You are guiding Priya through the chapter's fifth resistance step. First, study the two authority figures and decide which one actually deserves obedience. Then, when Coach Rex escalates and orders Priya to sign off on skipped medication checks, choose how she should respond.
key_concepts: The fifth step of resistance is to respect just authority but rebel against unjust authority.
Just authority rests on expertise, wisdom, seniority, or special status that genuinely deserves respect.
Unjust authority figures demand obedience without having any substance behind it.
Many who assume the mantle of authority are pseudo-leaders, false prophets, and confidence men who should not be respected but rather disobeyed and openly exposed to critical evaluation.
Parents, teachers, and religious leaders should teach children to distinguish deserved authority from undeserved authority, resisting authorities whose priorities are not in our best interests.
Resisting unjust authority reduces mindless obedience to self-proclaimed authorities.
Diffusion of responsibility merely disguises our individual complicity in questionable actions, so maintaining personal responsibility makes obedience to authority less blind.
Refusing to allow displacement of responsibility undercuts conformity to antisocial group norms.
The chapter advises always imagining a future time when today's deed will be on trial and no one will accept pleas of 'only following orders' or 'everyone else was doing it.'
The three Ss — self-awareness, situational sensitivity, and street smarts — are the key to resistance, and distinguishing authority types demands situational sensitivity.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the distinction between just and unjust authority: obedience is only justified when authority rests on expertise, wisdom, or special status, while authority without substance deserves active disobedience and exposure. The chapter frames this discrimination as central to reducing mindless obedience, especially under diffusion of responsibility.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests 'I respect just authority but rebel against unjust authority': earned authority (expertise, wisdom, seniority) deserves obedience, while self-promoting pseudo-leaders deserve open resistance and critical exposure, because blind obedience to them is the gateway to harm.
assets.stage_1_observation: Priya must decide whom to trust. Dr. Feld earns his authority through decades of careful practice and patient outcomes; Coach Rex's authority is manufactured by a consultant's contract and a performance bonus for the administrator. On screen, Rex's clipboard shows checklists crossed out in red ink while Feld's verification binder sits intact, and a caption reminds Priya that authority without substance deserves no obedience.
assets.stage_1_question: What distinguishes the authority Priya should obey from the one she should resist?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Just authority deserves respect because of its expertise, wisdom, seniority, or special status, whereas unjust authority demands obedience without any substance — so pseudo-leaders and self-promoters should be disobeyed and openly exposed to critical evaluation, not obeyed.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Coach Rex corners Priya in the med room and orders her to sign off on skipped medication double-checks, invoking 'the administrator's authority,' the ward's budget, and her own job security, and noting that 'everyone else signs.' He slides the clipboard at her. Priya must act now.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Priya refuses the order, states plainly that the verification checklist exists for patient safety and that she is personally responsible for her signature, and reports Rex's instruction to the hospital compliance office in writing — polite and courteous where justified, but disobedient to an authority whose priorities are not in the patients' best interests, and careful to avoid letting 'everyone else does it' displace her individual responsibility.

assets.topic: Individuation Versus the Anonymous Night Crew
assets.visual_frame_description: A cavernous warehouse loading dock on a Friday night. New hires wear identical gray coveralls, dark sunglasses, and temporary ID stickers bearing only numbers. Crew lead Dante, the only one without sunglasses, watches a laughing circle of coworkers drag Tomas, a shy temp, toward the open door of a walk-in freezer while chanting 'initiation.' Tomas's name tag is covered by tape; he is just 'the new one.'
assets.player_mission: You are helping Dante hold the line against a deindividuated crew. First, observe how anonymity strips Tomas of his identity and identify why that makes the 'prank' escalation so dangerous. Then, when the crew turns on Dante, choose the intervention that restores individuation and stops the freezer door from closing.
key_concepts: The fourth resistance step is 'I am Me, the best I can be': do not allow others to deindividuate you, put you in a category, or turn you into an object.
Anonymity and secrecy conceal wrongdoing and undermine the human connection.
Anonymity and secrecy are the breeding grounds that generate dehumanization.
Dehumanization provides the killing ground for bullies, rapists, torturers, terrorists, and tyrants.
Asserting your individuality means politely stating your name and credentials, loud and clear, and insisting on the same behavior in others.
Making eye contact — and removing eye-concealing sunglasses — reinforces unique identity and restores the human connection.
Offering information about yourself that reinforces your unique identity counters being reduced to a category or a slot.
Never allow or practice negative stereotyping; words, labels, and jokes can be destructive when they mock others.
Work to change whatever social conditions make people feel anonymous, and support practices that make others feel special and valued.
The fundamental attribution error locates the inner qualities of people as the main source of their actions, but the chapter argues situational variables such as anonymity transform actors.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests individuation as a resistance strategy: anonymity and secrecy breed dehumanization, so reasserting individual identity through names, eye contact, and the removal of concealing gear undercuts the deindividuated momentum of a group. The chapter's 'I am Me' step directly counters the SPE dynamics in which uniforms and numbers transformed ordinary men.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests 'I am Me, the best I can be': deindividuation strips people of identity and breeds dehumanization, so resistance means asserting names, making eye contact, refusing objectification, and breaking the anonymity that lets a group's worst norms take over.
assets.stage_1_observation: The night crew's transformation is visible on screen: identical coveralls, number-only ID stickers, sunglasses hiding every gaze, and Tomas reduced to 'the new one' with his name tag taped over. A caption recalls that anonymity and secrecy conceal wrongdoing and undermine the human connection, and that these are the breeding grounds of dehumanization.
assets.stage_1_question: Why does the anonymity of number-only IDs, identical uniforms, and eye-concealing sunglasses make the freezer 'prank' more dangerous than it looks?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Anonymity and secrecy conceal wrongdoing and undermine the human connection; they are the breeding grounds that generate dehumanization, and dehumanization provides the killing ground for bullying and cruelty — so the anonymous crew can treat Tomas as an object instead of a person.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The crew turns to Dante: 'Lighten up, it's just a prank — everyone's doing it.' Two workers are already pulling Tomas's arms toward the freezer door. Dante must break the deindividuated momentum in the next ten seconds. Choose his intervention.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Dante steps between the crew and the freezer, calls Tomas by his name, states his own name and job title loudly, pulls off his sunglasses to make eye contact with each crew member in turn, and physically blocks the door — refusing the 'just a prank' framing and refusing to let anyone be treated as an anonymous object. Making eye contact and reasserting individual identity is exactly the individuation strategy the chapter prescribes, and it converts 'everyone' back into named individuals who can be held responsible.

assets.visual_frame_description: A gray office in a military logistics depot in 2004. Wes, a young clerk, holds a CD of photographs showing detainees being abused by members of his own unit. On his screen, a pyramid of naked prisoners and a man on a leash glow in night-vision green. His sergeant's desk sits outside the office door; across the courtyard is the Criminal Investigation Division annex with its plain manila envelope drop box. A wall clock reads 2:10 a.m.
assets.player_mission: You are walking Wes through the hardest decision in the chapter: whether dissent becomes heroism only when it changes the system. First, study what the Milgram analysis says about merely objecting or walking away. Then, when his sergeant confronts him, choose the action that translates individual disobedience into systemic change.
key_concepts: In the Milgram research, verbal dissent was only ego balm for the 'teacher,' making him feel better about the terrible things he was doing to his 'learner.'

Behavioral disobedience was necessary to challenge authority, but in the Milgram experiment there was never disobedience more significant than a silent retreat as each teacher exited without changing anything.

One third of the original Milgram participants disobeyed and refused to go all the way, yet if the cover story were real, their silent refusal would not prevent the next 999 participants from experiencing the same distress.
Disobedience by the individual must be translated into systemic disobedience that forces change in the situation or agency itself, not just in some operating conditions.
It is too easy for evil situations to co-opt good dissidents by giving them medals for their deeds and a gift certificate for keeping their opinions to themselves.
Joe Darby, a lowly Army Reserve specialist, turned in the Abu Ghraib photos after the images stopped seeming funny and 'didn't sit right' for three days.
Darby chose between 'what I knew was morally right and my loyalty to other soldiers,' handed the disc to the Criminal Investigation Division anonymously, and gave a sworn statement.
Darby's act brought the abuses to a halt, triggered formal investigations, and led to significant changes in how Abu Ghraib Prison was run.
Whistle-blowers face retaliation: Darby and his family spent years in military protective custody after Secretary Rumsfeld revealed his identity.

Ridenhour exposed the My Lai massacre by sending letters to President Nixon and the Departments of Defense and Army insisting on a public investigation, and persisted until his righteous cause was recognized.

The tenth resistance step is 'I can oppose unjust systems': individual resistance in concert with others of the same mind and resolve can make a difference, and documenting all allegations of wrongdoing is part of it.
Heroism requires that an act be voluntary, involve risk or potential sacrifice, serve one or more other people or the community, and be without secondary extrinsic gain anticipated at the time.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the chapter's core claim about heroic dissent: individual refusal without systemic consequence is merely ego balm, as in Milgram, where even the disobedient third left silently. Real heroism translates disobedience into systemic disobedience that changes the institution, as Joe Darby's anonymous report of the Abu Ghraib photos did.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests whether dissent becomes heroism only when it changes the system: verbal protest and silent retreat are ego balm, while whistle-blowing that forces institutional change — like Darby's report of the Abu Ghraib abuses — is systemic disobedience.
assets.stage_1_observation: Wes has sat on the CD for three days, and the images have shifted from funny to horrifying. His options are visible on screen as three doors: quit the job silently, confront his sergeant verbally, or place the disc in the CID manila envelope with a sworn statement. A caption recalls Darby's words: 'I had the choice between what I knew was morally right and my loyalty to other soldiers. I couldn't have it both ways.'
assets.stage_1_question: According to the chapter's analysis of the Milgram experiment, why is Wes simply objecting and then walking away an inadequate response?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Verbal dissent was only ego balm for the Milgram 'teacher,' and the one third who disobeyed and refused to go all the way merely retreated silently — an isolated event without social impact, since it did not prevent the next participants from suffering and did not challenge the entire structure and assumptions of the research.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Wes's sergeant slams his hand on the desk, demanding the disc: 'You were never here. Loyalty means keeping quiet. You resign, everyone forgets.' The sergeant slides a resignation form across the desk while the clock ticks. Wes has the disc in his pocket and the CID drop box across the courtyard. Choose his action.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Wes refuses to hand over the disc, declines the silent resignation, and delivers the evidence to the Criminal Investigation Division with a sworn statement, accepting that retaliation will follow — exactly as Darby did when he burned a copy, typed an anonymous letter, and swore to Agent Tyler Pieron that he was the one who put the disc in the envelope. Individual disobedience must be translated into systemic disobedience that forces change in the institution itself, even at the cost of protective custody and ostracism.

assets.topic: The Phony Police Caller at the Fast-Food Counter
assets.visual_frame_description: A fast-food restaurant at 9 p.m., fluorescent lights over empty booths. Sarah Whitfield, 24, in a manager's uniform, stands at the counter phone, gripping the receiver while a teenage cashier watches her nervously and shakes her head. A sidebar on screen documents the hoax's reach — a dozen restaurant chains, nearly seventy establishments, thirty-two states — and a caption reads: 'Unless you are in that situation, at that time, how do you know what you would do?'
assets.player_mission: Audit the recorded interaction between Sarah and the caller. Compare her observed behavior during the call to her normal baseline, weigh the interrogation transcript, and deliver a verdict on what is actually happening to her and name the mechanism at work.
key_concepts: A phony-authority hoax duped many fast-food restaurant personnel into blindly following a false authority — in a dozen different restaurant chains across nearly seventy different establishments in thirty-two states.

The assistant manager in a McDonald's who was totally duped by the phony caller asks: 'Unless you are in that situation, at that time, how do you know what you would do? You don't know what you would do.'
Instead of distancing ourselves from the deceived by assuming negative dispositional attributes like stupidity or naivete, we need to understand why and how people like us were so completely seduced.
Understanding how the deception works puts us in a position to resist and to spread awareness of methods of resisting such hoaxes.
The caller's authority was manufactured: a police title, official-sounding jargon, and the threat of being 'held personally responsible' supplied symbols of legitimacy without substance.
Obedience to authority becomes less blind when we maintain a sense of personal responsibility and refuse to displace it onto the authority figure.
The three Ss — self-awareness, situational sensitivity, and street smarts — are the key to resisting unwanted influence.
A full 12 percent of Americans are defrauded by con-artist criminals each year, sometimes losing their life savings.
The detachment-versus-saturation duality means that the more open we are to other people's persuasion, the more likely we are to be swayed by it.
The illusion of personal invulnerability — 'Them? Yes. Me? No!' — leaves people convinced they are the special case, with their defenses down and their tail twisted.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests obedience to false authority: symbols of legitimacy — a police title, official jargon, and threats of personal responsibility — override normal judgment, exactly as in the McDonald's hoax that duped employees in nearly seventy establishments across thirty-two states. The chapter insists the deceived are not stupid but are seduced by situational forces any of us could face, and that understanding the seduction is the first step to resistance.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Is the assistant manager on the phone being influenced, threatened, or simply misinformed? Diagnose the interaction and identify the mechanism at work.
assets.subject_baseline: Sarah Whitfield, 24, assistant manager of a fast-food restaurant on the night shift. By every account she is level-headed and punctual, follows the manager's handbook strictly, has never been disciplined, and is well-liked by the teenage crew she supervises.
observed_nonverbal_log: 9:02 PM — The caller identifies himself as 'Officer Scott from the local police department.' Sarah's brow furrows; she mouths 'police' to the cashier, then straightens her posture.

9:04 PM — The caller claims a female employee stole a customer's cash and that Sarah must 'detain and strip-search' the suspect. Sarah grips the counter phone, swallows hard, and glances at the teenage crew member at the register.
9:07 PM — After the caller invokes 'the manager's authority' and warns she will be 'held personally responsible,' Sarah's voice drops, and she begins taking notes and nodding in agreement.
9:09 PM — Sarah motions the crew member toward the back room, face pale. The cashier shakes her head 'no,' but Sarah insists, keeping the phone pressed to her ear.
interrogation_transcript: Interviewer: Why did you keep following the instructions after it felt wrong?
Sarah: He was a police officer. Officers have authority. I thought — if I didn't do it, I'd be the one in trouble for obstruction.
Interviewer: Did you try to verify the caller at any point?
Sarah: It happened so fast. He knew the store. He used official words. I've never been through anything like this.
assets.correct_diagnosis: Obedience to a false, phony authority: Sarah is completely duped by the caller, in the same way that the phony-authority hoax duped employees in a dozen restaurant chains across nearly seventy establishments in thirty-two states.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The caller used no physical threat and no money demand; his levers were the symbols of legitimate authority — the police title, official-sounding jargon, and the threat of 'being held responsible' — plus manufactured urgency. Sarah's anxious compliance, note-taking, and insistence despite the cashier's objection reveal obedience to authority symbols, not malice and not misinformation. The chapter insists we understand why people like us are so completely seduced instead of assuming stupidity or naivete, so that we can resist and spread methods of resisting such hoaxes.
distractors: Sarah is willfully malicious and enjoys humiliating subordinates — her clean record and anxious, uncertain affect during the call contradict a cruel disposition, and the chapter rejects dispositional blame in favor of situational understanding.

The caller is genuinely a police officer running a legitimate investigation — no badge number, no supervisor callback, and a demand for a strip-search of an employee on a phone call violates any plausible protocol, so this is the signature of a hoax.

Sarah is being blackmailed by a caller with personal leverage over her — no leverage or threat is present; the only pressure is the manufactured authority of the police title and the threat of being held responsible.

assets.topic: The Lottery Wire Transfer and the Twelve Percent
assets.visual_frame_description: A tidy kitchen in a suburban Ohio home at 10:15 a.m. Doris Mahoney, 68, sits at the table with the cordless phone to her ear, a wire-transfer form in front of her and a checkbook half open. A timer overlay on screen marks each minute of the call, while a caption notes that a full 12 percent of Americans are defrauded by con-artist criminals each year, many of them over fifty.
assets.player_mission: Audit the phone call between Doris and the caller. Track her nonverbal responses against her baseline, weigh the interrogation transcript, and deliver a verdict on whether this is a legitimate prize disbursement or a confidence scheme.
key_concepts: A full 12 percent of Americans are defrauded by con-artist criminals each year, sometimes losing their life savings, and the majority of those defrauded are over fifty years old.
People of all ages are regularly duped by tricksters in telemarketing, health care, and lottery scams.
The three Ss — self-awareness, situational sensitivity, and street smarts — are the key to resisting unwanted influence, and the deadline tell is caught by situational sensitivity.
Urgency and deadlines are signature levers of confidence games: the caller's noon deadline manufactured panic that overrode Doris's verification instinct.
We are averse to things framed as potential losses, so the imagined loss of $2.3 million outweighed the real risk of losing $4,500.
We desire things that are framed as 'scarce' even when they are plentiful — here, a prize Doris never bought a ticket to win.
Critical thinking is part of resistance: ask for evidence to support assertions and separate rhetoric from substance.
The detachment-versus-saturation duality means that the more open we are to persuasion, the more likely we are to be swayed by it.
The illusion of personal invulnerability — 'Them? Yes. Me? No!' — leaves people convinced they are the special case, caught with their defenses down.
Admitting mistakes openly reduces the need to justify them and undercuts the motivation to keep supporting bad decisions.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the confidence game's three levers — false legitimacy, manufactured urgency, and loss framing — which together override verification instincts and defraud the 12 percent of Americans taken by con artists each year. The chapter's antidote is the three Ss, with situational sensitivity catching the artificial deadline.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Is 'Pat' a legitimate broker helping Doris claim her winnings, or a con artist running a telemarketing lottery scheme? Diagnose the interaction.
assets.subject_baseline: Doris Mahoney, 68, retired school librarian, frugal and sharp with numbers but deeply trusting of anyone with a warm voice. Two years ago she lost part of her late husband's pension fund to a 'grandchild emergency' scam and is ashamed of it.
observed_nonverbal_log: 10:15 AM — The caller, 'Pat from the national lottery commission,' tells Doris she has won $2.3 million. Doris laughs and says, 'I never bought a ticket,' but her hands are steady and she listens.

10:18 AM — Pat explains she must 'pay the processing fee' of $4,500 by wire transfer to release the winnings. Doris's lips tighten; she repeats 'processing fee' twice, then begins writing the wire instructions down.

10:22 AM — Pat adds urgency: 'This offer expires at noon; if you delay, the prize goes to someone else.' Doris's voice wavers; she reaches for her checkbook, then stops and starts to dial her bank branch — a flicker of her old prudence.
10:24 AM — Doris says, 'It's a lot of money, but if I don't act, I lose it.' Her hand is on the wire form and she has not verified the claim with anyone.
interrogation_transcript: Interviewer: What made you keep talking after you knew you never bought a ticket?
Doris: He knew my name, my address. He said the commission had my records. And the deadline — if I hung up, I'd lose it all.
Interviewer: Did you verify anything with the lottery commission?
Doris: There wasn't time. He said noon. I panicked.
assets.correct_diagnosis: A classic telemarketing confidence game operating on false legitimacy and manufactured urgency: Doris is about to become one of the 12 percent of Americans defrauded by con-artist criminals each year, many of them over fifty, in lottery-style scams.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The con runs on three levers: fake legitimacy (he knows her name, address, and claims official records), manufactured scarcity and urgency ('expires at noon,' 'the prize goes to someone else'), and the asymmetry of loss framing — Doris reacts to the imagined loss of winnings more than the actual risk of $4,500. Her panic overrode her verification instinct, which is precisely why the chapter's antidote is the three Ss: self-awareness of the panic, situational sensitivity to the deadline tell, and street smarts about a basic rule — legitimate lotteries never demand advance wire fees from winners.
distractors: The caller is a legitimate lottery official and the fee is routine — legitimate lotteries deduct taxes from prizes and never demand advance wire fees from winners, so the fee demand is the defining tell of the con.
Doris is being blackmailed by someone with personal leverage over her — no threat or leverage exists; the only pressure is the lure of winnings combined with an artificial deadline.

Doris is lying about the interaction to cover up her own embezzlement — her record is clean, and the scripted pattern of records, fee, and deadline matches the documented telemarketing fraud pattern rather than any diversion.

assets.visual_frame_description: A Jerusalem courtroom in 1961, the defendant enclosed in a glass dock. Adolf Eichmann, thin, bespectacled, in a suit, adjusts his papers with clerk-like precision as prosecutors gesture at charts of deportation routes. A subtitle strip tracks the psychiatrists' reports — 'normal,' 'not only normal but most desirable' — while the caption above the dock reads: 'The trouble with Eichmann was precisely that so many were like him.'
assets.player_mission: Audit Eichmann's demeanor and testimony at trial. Decide whether his flat, meticulous calm conceals a sadistic pathology or reveals something unsettling about ordinary people, then deliver your diagnosis of the mechanism Hannah Arendt identified.
key_concepts: Hannah Arendt formulated the banality of evil from her observations at the trial of Adolf Eichmann, indicted for crimes against humanity because he helped orchestrate the genocide of European Jews.
Arendt argued such individuals should not be viewed as exceptions, monsters, or perverted sadists, because such dispositional attributes set them apart from the rest of the human community.
Half a dozen psychiatrists certified Eichmann as 'normal' — one exclaiming he was 'more normal, at any rate, than I am after having examined him.'
Eichmann's defense was that he was simply following orders, and he remembered perfectly well that he would have had a bad conscience only if he had not done what he had been ordered to do.
Arendt concluded that the many who were like Eichmann were neither perverted nor sadistic but 'terribly and terrifyingly normal.'
From the viewpoint of legal institutions and moral standards, this normality was much more terrifying than all the atrocities put together.
The new type of criminal commits his crimes under circumstances that make it almost impossible for him to know or feel that he is doing wrong.

Christopher Browning's Reserve Police Battalion 101 — middle-aged, working-class family men from Hamburg — shot thousands of unarmed Jews and arranged the deportation of thousands more; they were all 'ordinary men.'
Ervin Staub's research concluded that 'evil that arises out of ordinary thinking and is committed by ordinary people is the norm, not the exception.'
Zygmunt Bauman believed cruelty should be attributed to its social origins more than to 'characterological' determinants or faulty personalities.
John Conroy, who studied men involved in torture in Ireland, Israel, and Chicago, concluded that 'unspeakable acts' were committed by 'ordinary people.'
Arendt's punch line: Eichmann's dignified march to the gallows summed up the lesson of 'the fearsome, word-and-thought-defying banality of evil.'
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the banality of evil: Eichmann's terrifying normalcy, certified by psychiatrists, shows that the architects of genocide need no monstrous disposition — only ordinary obedience to orders. Arendt's conclusion that the many were neither perverted nor sadistic anchors the chapter's claim that ordinary people, not monsters, commit atrocity.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Is the defendant on trial a sadistic monster whose pathology explains the genocide, or something more unsettling? Diagnose the man in the glass dock.
assets.subject_baseline: Adolf Eichmann, the SS officer indicted for crimes against humanity for helping orchestrate the genocide of European Jews. No prior psychiatric history; a punctual, meticulous bureaucrat known for his zeal in organizing deportations by the numbers.
observed_nonverbal_log: 9:00 AM — Eichmann enters the glass dock, adjusts his papers precisely, and greets his lawyer with a small nod. His affect is flat but courteous, like a civil servant arriving at an office.
9:20 AM — Under questioning about deportation figures, he answers with precise, rehearsed numbers and dates, gesturing with both hands like a clerk citing ledgers; he shows no agitation.
9:45 AM — Asked about shipping children to their deaths, he pauses only to correct a minor figure. His voice does not rise; he appears to be testifying about logistics rather than murder.
10:05 AM — Asked whether he had a bad conscience, he states he would have had a bad conscience only if he had not done what he was ordered to do — delivered calmly, almost helpfully.
interrogation_transcript: Prosecutor: Are you aware of what your orders caused?
Eichmann: I was following orders. It was my duty. Had I not done it, I would have had a bad conscience.
Prosecutor: You have been called a monster. How do you see yourself?
Eichmann: I am not what you call an innerer Schweinehund — a dirty bastard in the depths of my heart. I am an ordinary man.
assets.correct_diagnosis: The banality of evil: Eichmann is not a perverted sadist but 'terribly and terrifyingly normal' — an ordinary bureaucrat whose very normalcy is more terrifying than the atrocities, exactly as Hannah Arendt concluded at his trial.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Half a dozen psychiatrists certified Eichmann as 'normal,' one exclaiming he was 'more normal, at any rate, than I am after having examined him,' and another finding his outlook toward family 'not only normal but most desirable.' Arendt's lesson is that treating perpetrators as monsters sets them apart from the human community and blinds us; exposing their ordinariness reveals that such people are a pervasive, hidden danger in all societies. Eichmann's calm, ledger-citing demeanor and his 'following orders' defense are the mechanism — ordinary obedience and meticulous duty, not pathology.
distractors: Eichmann is faking calm to deceive the court about a sadistic personality — the chapter's point is the opposite: his ordinariness is genuine and therefore more terrifying, and psychiatrists certified his normality.
Eichmann is a misunderstood scapegoat who did nothing wrong — he orchestrated the transports with zeal and meticulous care; the diagnosis concerns his psychological type, not his guilt.
Eichmann suffers from a psychotic delusion that the transports were humanitarian — no delusion is present; he knew exactly what the orders meant and executed them with meticulous care.

assets.visual_frame_description: A whitewashed training compound in Greece in 1969, under the military junta. Nineteen-year-old conscript Yannis stands in a line of recruits at dawn, chanting insults at a photograph of 'the enemy,' glancing sideways at his bunkmate for approval. A timeline strip at the bottom of the screen advances from week one to week twelve, marking each escalation in his drill routine, from shouted accusations to live strikes on bound prisoners.
assets.player_mission: Audit the twelve-week training cycle of the conscript Yannis. Compare his baseline to his behavior at each recorded stage and determine whether the evidence reveals a pre-existing sadist or a man made into a torturer by training, then deliver your diagnosis.
key_concepts: Mika Haritos-Fatouros concluded from her in-depth analysis of soldiers trained by the Greek military junta to be state-sanctioned torturers (1967–1974) that torturers are not born but made by their training.
'Anybody's son will do' was her answer to the question of who will make an effective torturer.
In a matter of months, ordinary young men from rural villages became 'weaponized' by their training in cruelty.
The trained men acted like brute beasts capable of inflicting the most horrendous acts of humiliation, pain, and suffering on anyone labeled 'the enemy.'
John Conroy, who studied men involved in torture in Ireland, Israel, and Chicago, concluded that in all cases 'unspeakable acts' were committed by 'ordinary people.'
Torturers act out the will of the community they represent in suppressing its foes.
The consensus among those who have studied torturers is that in general they were not distinguishable from the general population in background or disposition prior to taking on their sordid job.
The Brazilian junta's 'violence workers' — policemen who tortured and murdered other Brazilian citizens — were also 'ordinary men' on all the evidence.
Milgram's escalating-orders paradigm shows how compliance with small initial steps normalizes each subsequent, larger step.
Zygmunt Bauman's analysis holds that cruelty should be attributed to its social origins more than to 'characterological' determinants or faulty personalities.
Ervin Staub concluded that 'evil that arises out of ordinary thinking and is committed by ordinary people is the norm, not the exception.'
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the making of a torturer: Haritos-Fatouros's analysis of the Greek junta's training program shows that 'anybody's son will do' — ordinary men become weaponized through incremental escalation, not pre-existing pathology. The finding is echoed in Conroy's torturers in Ireland, Israel, and Chicago and in Brazil's violence workers.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Is the trainee being shaped into a torturer by training and system, or revealed as a pre-existing sadist? Diagnose the young conscript across the training cycle.
assets.subject_baseline: Yannis, 19, a village shepherd from rural northern Greece, conscripted in 1969 during the military junta years (1967–1974). No disciplinary record, no history of violence, quiet, and eager to please his drill instructors.
observed_nonverbal_log: Week 1, 6:00 AM — Barracks indoctrination: recruits chant insults at a photograph of 'the enemy.' Yannis hesitates, then joins the chant, glancing at his bunkmate afterward to check whether conformity is expected.
Week 4 — Interrogation drill with a hooded conscript playing the prisoner: Yannis is ordered to shout accusations. His voice shakes, and he looks at the instructor after every shout for approval.
Week 8 — Live session: ordered to strike a bound prisoner. Yannis hits, flinches, then hits again harder after the instructor nods. His breathing is fast and his jaw is set.
Week 12 — Solo duty: Yannis conducts a full beating routine without instruction, then reports to the sergeant for feedback on technique. His posture is confident and he no longer hesitates.
interrogation_transcript: Interviewer: Did you believe these men were your enemies?
Yannis: The instructors said so. They were all enemies of the state. I did what I was trained to do.
Interviewer: Did it ever feel wrong?
Yannis: At first. But everyone did it. You learn it becomes your job, like any job.
assets.correct_diagnosis: The torturer is made, not born: 'Anybody's son will do' — as Mika Haritos-Fatouros concluded from her analysis of the Greek military junta's state-sanctioned torture training, in which ordinary young men became weaponized in a matter of months.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Yannis's baseline shows no violent history, and his escalation tracks the training calendar: hesitant conformity in week one, instructor-seeking approval in week four, obedience after a nod in week eight, and autonomous brutality by week twelve. The consensus across venues — John Conroy's torturers in Ireland, Israel, and Chicago — is that torturers were not distinguishable from the general population before their jobs, and Haritos-Fatouros concluded that in a few months training made ordinary villagers capable of the most horrendous acts on anyone labeled 'the enemy.' The mechanism is incremental Milgram-style escalation plus normalized routine, and the same conclusion applied to the 'violence workers' of the Brazilian junta.
distractors: Yannis is a natural sadist whose village upbringing finally found an outlet — he had no history of violence, and the training itself produced the behavior, so 'anybody's son will do' is the correct reading.

Yannis is an unwilling victim of hypnotic control with no responsibility — the change came from incremental escalation, drills, and normalized routines, not hypnosis, and the chapter holds torturers responsible while explaining their making.

Yannis's cruelty proves the Greek population was uniquely brutal — identical patterns were found in Brazil's police violence workers and elsewhere, so the evidence points to training and system, not nationality.

assets.visual_frame_description: A sorting-board interface glows on screen: three columns labeled Physical-risk heroism, Social-risk heroism, and Pseudoheroism. Portrait cards of Richard Rescorla, Joe Darby, Nelson Mandela, Hugh Thompson, a reality-television star, a staged rescue, and Debbie Layton slide across the board as the player assigns each to a column, with a score counter ticking in the corner.
assets.player_mission: Classify each of the seven acts into the correct column. Watch for the distinction between risks to the body, risks to status and freedom, and media-created heroism with no sacrifice at all, then confirm your verdict on the target case of Joe Darby.
key_concepts: Becker and Eagly define heroes as 'individuals who choose to take risks on behalf of one or more other people, despite the possibility of dying or suffering serious physical consequences from these actions.'
Peter Martens challenged this narrow definition, noting it singled out only heroes who stood for an idea or principle.
John McCain contends that 'the standard of courage remains, as I think it should, acts that risk life or limb or other very serious personal injuries for the sake of others or to uphold a virtue.'
The risk component in heroism can be any serious threat to the quality of life — including loss of social or economic status, ostracism, career, or imprisonment.

Heroism has four key features: it must be voluntary, involve a risk or potential sacrifice, be conducted in service to one or more other people or the community, and be without secondary extrinsic gain anticipated at the time.
Physical-risk heroism usually involves a probability, not the certainty, of serious injury or death, and the individual is generally removed from the situation after a short period.
The risk associated with physical-risk heroism is better termed peril, while the risk involved in civil heroism is considered sacrifice — costs that are not time-limited.
Daniel Boorstin deflated the confluence of heroism with celebrity: 'vainly do we make scores of artificial celebrities grow where nature planted only a single hero.'
Pseudoheroes are media creations promoted by powerful systemic forces, and hero status is sometimes conferred when not deserved by the actions.
If secondary gains are accrued after the act without prior anticipation of or motivation to attain them, the act still qualifies as heroic.
Joe Darby's whistle-blowing was a social-risk act in service to the community, and his later honors, including the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award, came without being anticipated.
Richard Rescorla is credited with saving the lives of about 2,800 Morgan Stanley employees in World Trade Center Tower 2 before it collapsed, dying when the building imploded.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the chapter's taxonomy of heroism: physical-risk acts, social-risk civil heroism involving threats to quality of life, and pseudoheroism as media-created celebrity. Drawing on Eagly, Becker, Martens, and McCain, the chapter broadens heroism beyond the battlefield to include whistle-blowers like Darby.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Classify each act into its column. The target case is Joe Darby, the Army Reservist who exposed the Abu Ghraib abuses: which column does his heroism belong in?

rows.label: Richard Rescorla evacuating roughly 2,800 Morgan Stanley employees from World Trade Center Tower 2 on 9/11, dying when the building imploded
Joe Darby turning in the Abu Ghraib photos despite expecting retaliation from soldiers in his own company
A reality-television personality celebrated as a hero solely for being famous, with no sacrifice or risk
Nelson Mandela enduring twenty-seven years of imprisonment on Robben Island for opposing apartheid
Warrant Officer Hugh Thompson flying his helicopter between American soldiers and wounded villagers at My Lai and threatening to open fire on his own troops to stop the massacre
A celebrity's public-relations team engineering a staged 'heroic rescue' on camera for ratings
Debbie Layton fleeing Jonestown to file a sworn affidavit warning the U.S. government of an imminent mass suicide

distractors: a — Darby risked no physical harm, so his act must be physical-risk heroism. No: Becker and Eagly's narrow physical-risk definition was challenged because risk can be any serious threat to quality of life, and Darby's defining risk was ostracism, retaliation, and years of protective custody.

c — Darby became famous, so he must be a media-created pseudohero. No: his awards, including the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award, came after the act without prior anticipation; he expected retaliation, not reward, and anticipated secondary gain would disqualify an act.
a and b — Darby risked both life and status. No: each item sorts to exactly one column in this matrix, and his case is the canonical social-risk exemplar in the chapter.
assets.explanation: Physical-risk heroism involves the possibility of death or serious physical injury, as with Rescorla and Thompson; social-risk heroism involves threats to career, status, freedom, or quality of life, as with Darby, Mandela, and Layton; pseudoheroism is Daniel Boorstin's media-created celebrity or an agency-promoted hero with no real sacrifice. Darby's act was voluntary, in service to others, and carried risk of retaliation rather than physical danger, and his later recognition came without being anticipated — so it sorts to social-risk heroism.

assets.visual_frame_description: A three-column sorting board labeled Self-awareness, Situational sensitivity, and Street smarts. Cards with short quotes — 'I'm sorry; I apologize; forgive me,' Langer's automatic pilot, Richard Clark's discrepancy detectors, the 'death tax' slogan — slide into place as the player sorts each resistance move under its dominant S, while a highlighted card reads: 'Them? Yes. Me? No!'
assets.player_mission: Sort each resistance move under its dominant S. Then answer the target question: which of the three Ss defeats the illusion that you are personally immune to situational influence?
key_concepts: The key to resistance lies in development of the three Ss: self-awareness, situational sensitivity, and street smarts.
The illusion of personal invulnerability — 'Them? Yes. Me? No!' — is defeated by applying the lessons learned about others to oneself.

In the face of strong, common situational forces, individual differences shrink and are compressed, so behavioral scientists can predict what the majority will do knowing only the nature of their behavioral context.
The 'I made a mistake' step says the six magic words — 'I'm sorry'; 'I apologize'; 'Forgive me' — and cuts bait instead of staying the course when a decision was wrong.
Confession of error undercuts the motivation to reduce cognitive dissonance; dissonance evaporates when a reality check occurs.
Ellen Langer's mindfulness transforms mindless inattention into mindfulness, especially in new situations, instead of living on automatic pilot.
The 'I am responsible' step refuses to allow diffusion or displacement of responsibility, because diffusion merely disguises individual complicity.
Richard Clark's street smarts — his 'discrepancy detectors' and intuition — let him read Jonestown's signs and escape to safety with eight others.
Zimbardo's South Bronx childhood taught him street smarts: figuring out quickly how certain people would be likely to act in certain situations.
Frame vigilance demands critical thinking: ask for evidence, separate rhetoric from substance, and reject simple solutions as quick fixes.
Taking personal responsibility puts the actor in the driver's seat and refuses to let 'only following orders' or 'everyone else was doing it' excuse complicity.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the three Ss of resistance — self-awareness, situational sensitivity, and street smarts — which the chapter presents as the key to resisting unwanted influence. The illusion of personal invulnerability is defeated by self-awareness, because strong situational forces compress individual differences in everyone, not just 'those others.'

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Each resistance move rests mainly on one of the three Ss. The target challenge is the illusion of personal invulnerability — 'Them? Yes. Me? No!' — which of the three Ss defeats it?

rows.label: Saying the six magic words — 'I'm sorry'; 'I apologize'; 'Forgive me' — when a decision you made was wrong
Applying Ellen Langer's mindfulness instead of running on automatic pilot in a new situation
Richard Clark reading Jonestown's tell-tale signs — no one smiling, everyone hungry, people whispering — and trusting his 'discrepancy detectors'
Taking personal responsibility and refusing to let the group diffuse it by saying 'only following orders'
Being frame-vigilant about slogans like 'death tax' that feel like plain facts rather than frames
Zimbardo's South Bronx apprenticeship in learning to predict how certain people would be likely to act in certain situations
Confessing an error openly so that dissonance evaporates instead of motivating continued support for a bad action

distractors: b — noticing the illusion requires reading situations. No: the invulnerability illusion is a blind spot about one's own susceptibility, so self-awareness, not situational reading, is the corrective the chapter describes.
c — street smarts would detect it. No: street smarts read other people's tactics; the invulnerability illusion concerns the self, so it is defeated by self-awareness.
a and c — both are equally required. No: each item in this matrix sorts to exactly one dominant S, and the chapter anchors the invulnerability illusion to the first S.
assets.explanation: The key to resistance is the development of the three Ss: self-awareness, situational sensitivity, and street smarts. The illusion of personal invulnerability — 'Them? Yes. Me? No!' — is defeated by self-awareness: it is hard to extend lessons learned abstractly about 'those others' to one's own conduct, yet common situational forces compress individual differences, so the aware person assumes the lessons apply to themselves.

assets.topic: Ordinary People, Two Banalities, One Myth
assets.visual_frame_description: A dark museum-like gallery with three display cases labeled Banality of evil, Banality of heroism, and the Hero-gene myth. Photographs and evidence cards — Eichmann in his glass dock, Battalion 101's family men, the righteous Gentiles hiding Dutch Jews, Joe Darby in uniform, Achilles in armor — slide into the cases as the player assigns each to its column.
assets.player_mission: Sort each case into its column. Then answer the target question about Adolf Eichmann, deciding whether his ordinariness belongs to the banality of evil, the banality of heroism, or the hero-gene myth.
key_concepts: Hannah Arendt's banality of evil emerged from her observations at the trial of Adolf Eichmann, who helped orchestrate the genocide of European Jews.
Eichmann was 'terribly and terrifyingly normal' — neither perverted nor sadistic — and his normality was more terrifying than all the atrocities put together.
Christopher Browning's Reserve Police Battalion 101 — middle-aged, working-class family men sent from Hamburg — shot thousands of unarmed Jews; they were all 'ordinary men.'
Ervin Staub concluded that 'evil that arises out of ordinary thinking and is committed by ordinary people is the norm, not the exception.'
The banality of heroism holds that doers of heroic deeds of the moment are not essentially different from those who comprise the base rate of the easily seduced.
The banality of goodness describes European Christians who helped Jews during the Holocaust, acting out of a sense of common decency without considering themselves heroic.
The hero-gene myth is the romantic view that heroes are supermen and -women born with a hero gene, a cut or more above the common breed.
Joe Darby, an ordinary bullied kid from a poor family in the Allegheny Mountains, stopped the Abu Ghraib abuses by turning in the photos.
Zygmunt Bauman believed the exception to the norm is the rare individual who has the capacity to assert moral autonomy in resisting destructive authorities.
The Greek junta's torturers were ordinary village boys 'weaponized' into brute beasts by a few months of training in cruelty.
Both evil and heroism emerge in particular situations when situational forces move a person across a decisional line from inaction to action.
The chapter urges fostering a 'heroic imagination,' conveying that every person is a hero in waiting who will be counted upon to do the right thing when the moment of decision comes.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the symmetry of the two banalities: ordinary people commit both atrocity and heroism, while the hero-gene myth wrongly locates both in exceptional dispositions. Arendt's Eichmann and Browning's Battalion 101 anchor the banality of evil; Darby and the righteous Gentiles anchor the banality of goodness.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: The chapter contrasts two banalities with the romantic hero myth. The target case is Adolf Eichmann, 'terribly and terrifyingly normal': which column does he belong in?

rows.label: Adolf Eichmann, certified 'normal' by half a dozen psychiatrists, shipping millions of men, women, and children to their deaths with great zeal and meticulous care
The middle-aged family men of Reserve Police Battalion 101, sent from Hamburg, shooting thousands of unarmed Jews in Polish villages
European Christians who hid Dutch Jews during the Holocaust, acting out of a sense of common decency without considering themselves heroic
The belief that heroes are supermen and -women, 'a cut or more above the common breed,' born with a hero gene
Joe Darby, an ordinary, bullied kid from the Allegheny Mountains, stopping the Abu Ghraib abuses by turning in the photos
Achilles, the archetypal war hero whose godlike exceptionality, in the Aristotelian view, transcends moral judgment and constitutional control
The Greek junta's torturers, ordinary village boys 'weaponized' into brute beasts by a few months of training in cruelty

distractors: b — his trial made him famous, so his evil is a kind of heroism. No: Arendt's banality of evil is precisely about normal perpetrators, not about glory; Eichmann's ordinariness was the horror, and no heroic quality is involved.

c — only an exceptional monster could have done this. No: the hero-gene myth is the dispositional error applied to good people, and Arendt's point is that no exceptional disposition is needed for evil either — the many who were like him were neither perverted nor sadistic.
a and c — he is both normal and exceptional. No: each case sorts to exactly one column; the chapter insists evil arising from ordinary thinking by ordinary people is the norm, not the exception.
assets.explanation: Arendt's banality of evil describes perpetrators like Eichmann and Battalion 101 whose ordinariness — not pathology — enabled atrocities, culminating in 'the fearsome, word-and-thought-defying banality of evil.' The banality of heroism and goodness describes ordinary rescuers and doers of good who 'did what had to be done,' like the righteous Gentiles and Joe Darby. The hero-gene myth is the romantic view that heroes are exceptional beings. Ervin Staub's research concludes that 'evil that arises out of ordinary thinking and is committed by ordinary people is the norm, not the exception.'
